food.title: Eating what you grow
food.bitter-cucurbits: Squash, melon or cucumber that tastes bitter can be poisonous. Stop eating it, and do not save its seed. Grow ornamental gourds away from food squash, since crosses with them can bring bitterness in. Follow your national food-safety authority’s guidance.
food.dry-beans: Dry beans and other pulses are not safe to eat raw or undercooked. Follow your national food-safety authority’s guidance on preparing them.
food.nightshades: The nightshade family, which includes tomatoes, potatoes, eggplants, peppers and their wild relatives, has poisonous members and poisonous parts. Eat only the parts you know to be food, and follow your national food-safety authority’s guidance.
food.potato-berries: The small green berries that potato plants sometimes set look like little tomatoes but are poisonous. Never eat them, keep them away from children, and follow your national food-safety authority’s guidance.
food.corn-processing: Corn eaten as a staple, such as flour corn, is traditionally nixtamalized before it is eaten, a process that uses caustic materials. Do not improvise it: follow your national food-safety authority’s guidance.
food.treated-seed: Seed treated with fungicides or other chemicals, often dyed a bright colour, must never be eaten or fed to animals. Keep it apart from seed you might eat, and follow your national food-safety authority’s guidance.
food.fava: Fava beans can cause a serious reaction in people with an inherited condition called favism. If you or your family might have it, ask a doctor before eating them, and follow your national food-safety authority’s guidance.
food.ergot: Rye and other grains can carry ergot, a poisonous fungus that replaces some kernels with hard, dark bodies. Do not eat or mill grain that contains it, and follow your national food-safety authority’s guidance.
food.sprouted-or-surplus-seed: Seed kept for sowing is not always fit to eat or to sprout as food: it may have been treated, mixed or stored in ways food is not. Follow your national food-safety authority’s guidance before eating surplus seed or sprouts.
food.toxic-leaves: Some trees grown for their leaves are poisonous raw or undercooked, and a few stay harmful even when cooked. Eat leaves only from a species you have identified with certainty and know to be food, never eat them raw unless they are known to be safe raw, and follow your national food-safety authority’s guidance.
food.home-canning: Home canning of low-acid foods, such as squash, beans or corn, can cause botulism, a poisoning that can kill. Some foods, such as mashed squash, are not considered safe to can at home at all. Follow your national food-safety authority’s guidance before canning anything.
food.raw-tasting: Tasting raw or unfamiliar plant parts, even a small piece spat out, can poison you: crosses and wild relatives can carry toxins you cannot see or smell. Do not use your mouth as a test, keep it away from children, and follow your national food-safety authority’s guidance.
food.wild-foods: Wild plants and mushrooms are easily confused with poisonous or deadly look-alikes. Never eat one you have not identified with certainty, ideally with an expert in person, and follow your national food-safety authority’s guidance.

timeline.label: Through the year, by season
years.0.do: Sow a mix of many varieties together.
years.1.do: Most varieties fail. Save seed only from the plants that made it.
years.2.do: Sow the survivors’ seed. Natural crosses appear.
years.2.alt: Beans in the survivors’ colours, many of them two-toned.
years.3.do: Keep selecting. Add a new variety now and then.
years.3.alt: A varied population with one new variety added.
years.key: Faded beans are plants that set no seed. Two-tone beans are new crosses. The speckled purple bean in year 3 is a newly added variety.
plot.title.row-ends: One variety at each end of the row
plot.alt.blocks: Four varieties planted in four separate blocks.
plot.alt.mixed: The same four varieties planted mixed together.
plot.alt.row-ends: A row with one variety at each end and crossed plants where they meet in the middle.
plot.alt.colour-blocks: Three blocks of different colours side by side, with crossed plants only along the edges where they touch.
plot.caption.row-ends: Crosses turn up where the two varieties meet.
plot.caption.colour-blocks: Crossed seed appears only along the edges where two blocks touch.
flower.alt.tomato-closed: Side view of a garden tomato flower: a closed cone of anthers hides the stigma.
flower.alt.tomato-open: Side view of a wild-type tomato flower: loose anthers and a stigma sticking out, with a bee approaching.
flower.alt.squash-male: A male squash flower on a long thin stalk, with its anthers in the middle.
flower.alt.squash-female: A female squash flower with a small fruit below it and a stigma in the middle.
flower.alt.corn: A corn plant: the tassel at the top sheds pollen; the silks of the ear below catch it.
flower.alt.carrot-fertile: A carrot umbel of many small flowers, with one flower enlarged: five anthers full of pollen.
flower.alt.carrot-sterile: A carrot umbel of many small flowers, with one flower enlarged: the anthers are shrivelled and carry no pollen, as on a male-sterile plant.
flower.alt.spinach-male: A male spinach plant: clusters of small flowers up the top of the stem shed pollen on the wind.
flower.alt.spinach-female: A female spinach plant: small flowers in the leaf axils, each with short feathery stigmas, where the seed forms.

crop.cms.high: On his list of crops whose shop-bought hybrids are often pollen-sterile. Start from heirlooms or local seed, and check flowers for anthers and pollen.
crop.cms.flagged: He flags shop-bought hybrids of this crop as possibly pollen-sterile. Check flowers for anthers and pollen.
crop.cms.low: Shop-bought hybrids are usually a fine start, in his experience.
ease.why.very-easy: Annuals that cross freely. New combinations show up in the first year.
ease.why.easy: Annuals that cross often enough, or whose flowers are easy to cross by hand.
ease.why.hard: Mostly roots that must survive a winter before they flower, or crops with little diversity left.
ease.why.very-hard: Crops that rarely cross on their own, or that are hard to manage.
